messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Markus Weber is a 56-year-old combat pilot who came to treatment after months of telling himself he should be able to handle what happened. During a training flight the previous year, his aircraft suffered a catastrophic mechanical failure on descent. He remembered the first loud bang inside the cockpit, sharp and unnatural, followed by warning alarms and a violent shudder that threw his body against the harness. In the seconds before impact, he became acutely aware of his own physical sensations—lightheadedness, a sick rolling feeling in his stomach, the sense that his body was no longer reliable. He survived the crash, but the experience seemed to split his life into before and after. What stayed with him was not only the memory of the explosion-like sound and the disorientation in his body, but the conviction that the world could become lethal without warning.

In the weeks afterward, those same sensations began to feel less like ordinary bodily states and more like signals that danger was already underway. If he grew dizzy standing up too quickly, or felt vaguely unwell after a poor night’s sleep, his whole system seemed to snap tight. A slammed metal door on base or any bang resembling an explosion made him jolt before he could think. Around other people, even small unexpected movements in the room pulled a reflexive reaction out of him, as though he had to defend himself before he knew what he was seeing. He described living with his body “revved up,” constantly tense, scanning, watchful, unable to relax even at home with his wife. The dizziness and sick feeling frightened him not only because they resembled moments from the crash, but because they seemed to confirm what he had come to believe: that the world is dangerous, that the rules he trusted about skill and preparation no longer hold, and that he himself had become somehow hollowed out by the experience.

Those beliefs hardened over time. Markus had come to feel that what was destroyed in the crash was not just the aircraft, but his confidence in how life worked. He said there had always been risk in aviation, but now risk felt omnipresent, stripped of meaning or fairness. He moved through his days with a deadened quality that troubled him almost as much as the fear. He noticed that when dizziness or a sudden bang set him off, what followed was not only alarm but a bleak, immediate thought—of course this is what the world is, unsafe and ready to turn. In that state, even ordinary physical discomfort took on the force of evidence.

He began organizing his life around not setting off that chain. He avoided hospitals, ambulances, and physical examinations with unusual rigidity, even when he knew routine medical care would have been sensible. He could not bear waiting rooms, the smell of antiseptic, or the suggestion that someone might check his body closely; those situations made him too aware of feeling lightheaded or ill. At work he stayed functional, but he narrowed his world outside the cockpit. He gave up dinners out, stopped meeting friends for activities he had once enjoyed, and became strict and controlling about what he ate, telling himself that if he kept his body tightly managed he might prevent the sensations that sent him spiraling. The more on guard he felt, the more he relied on these routines. If his body was going to stay primed for danger, he believed he had to compensate by controlling every variable he could.

But these efforts tightened rather than relieved things. Restricting his eating left him physically depleted at times, and the resulting lightheadedness only made the old fear more immediate. Avoiding medical settings meant he never had the chance to learn that bodily sensations could be tolerated without catastrophe, so every spell of dizziness remained potent. Pulling out of enjoyable parts of life left him more emotionally flat, and that numbness fed his sense that something vital in him had died in the crash. His wife had started commenting that he was present in the house but unreachable; Markus heard the truth in that and felt ashamed, then withdrew further. He noticed, too, that the smaller his world became, the more sharply he reacted to sounds and movement within it. A dropped tool in the hangar, a cart clattering across concrete, someone stepping unexpectedly into his peripheral vision—each seemed to prove again that he could not let his guard down.

By the time he sought help, Markus was exhausted by the discipline it took to manage each day and frightened by how little of himself he could still feel. What finally brought him in was a recent physical exam he postponed twice, then abandoned after seeing an ambulance pull up outside the clinic and feeling instantly sick and lightheaded in the parking lot. He sat in his truck shaking, unable to go inside, and realized his life was being run by efforts to avoid that moment. He says he wants his marriage and ordinary life back, but what he fears most is that the crash revealed a permanent truth—that the world is fundamentally dangerous, his body cannot be trusted, and the part of him that once felt alive may not return.
